conversation.Statement: Hello! What can I help you with today?
I've been trying to understand how p-values work in statistics. Can you explain?

Of course! A p-value helps you determine the significance of your results in a hypothesis test. It represents the probability of observing the results, or something more extreme, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
So, if I get a small p-value, does that mean my hypothesis is definitely true?

Not exactly. A small p-value indicates that the observed data is unlikely under the null hypothesis, so you might reject it. But it doesn't prove your alternative hypothesis is true with absolute certainty.
That makes sense. How small does the p-value need to be to reject the null hypothesis?
Typically, a threshold called alpha is set, commonly at 0.05. If your p-value is less than alpha, you reject the null hypothesis. But this threshold can vary depending on the study or context.
What about confidence intervals? Are they related to p-values?
Yes! Confidence intervals provide a range of values within which the true parameter likely falls. They complement p-values by giving you an estimate range instead of just a probability.
Thanks for the clear explanation. This really helps me get a better grasp of basic statistics.
You're very welcome! Feel free to ask if you have more questions anytime.
